summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence and enhanced in the first post-independence penal code adopted in 2015. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. The same report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Foreign nationals are not shielded. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including Article 600 of the Penal Code. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual; the Eritrean ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action.

Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists; abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have been subjected to severe abuse, including physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed.

Criminalisation undermines health and care access. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an "area of concern." There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. The government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people," with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws. In 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles.
tangentialFactors:
The 2011 US State Department human rights report, relayed by Asmarino, records that societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred and that the government labelled disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles," indicating the accusation of homosexuality is used as a political smear. The 2010 US State Department report for Eritrea records criminalisation of same-sex conduct alongside torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, situating the anti-LGBTQ provision within a broader pattern of state repression rather than an isolated statute.

The UK Foreign Office raised concerns about Eritrea's treatment of LGBTQ people bilaterally and through the EU, but this diplomatic pressure has not produced legislative change. The UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported the death penalty was not used in Eritrea in 2013, though illegal executions of prisoners are reported.
localsOnly:
Eritrean residents face indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and torture as documented in the 2010 US State Department report, conditions that intersect with the criminalisation regime. The law on assault makes no gender distinction, per the 2023 US State Department report, but this does not offset the absence of any anti-discrimination protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded for Eritrea. There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military face severe abuse rests on a single 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed; corroboration from independent monitors is not sourced here. The reference to Article 600 of the Penal Code in the Paolo Mannina deportation corresponds to the older Ethiopian-era numbering, while the current provision is cited as Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code; whether these are the same substantive offence under renumbering is not resolved in the inventory.

The UK Foreign Office report carries a 2015 copyright date, so its statements about the absence of anti-discrimination legislation and about bilateral and EU representations may not reflect the current diplomatic position. Whether any change to Article 310(1) has been proposed or debated since the 2015 adoption is not sourced. No specific sentencing data or prosecution statistics for Article 310(1) are available in the inventory.
